usage: '키우다' (to raise) is the natural verb for having a pet, not '가지다'
particle '과/와' marks the dog as your companion on the walk
'동반' = accompanying; you'll see this sign on pet-friendly venues
Koreans say '우리' (our) even for personal pets; very natural
examples: 저는 반려견을 한 마리 키우고 있어요.
'동반이 가능하다' = accompaniment is possible, common venue phrasing
dog registration ('반려견 등록') is legally required in Korea
nuance: '반려견' is the warm, modern word for a pet dog, literally 'companion dog,' and it has largely replaced the older '애완견' which sounds like the dog is a possession or toy. Use '반려견' in any polite or official context; in casual speech people just say '강아지' regardless of the dog's age.
mistakes: Saying '애완견' — it now sounds outdated and slightly disrespectful; '반려견' is preferred
Using '가지다' (to have/own) instead of '키우다' (to raise) for owning a pet

usage: '입양하다' (to adopt) is increasingly preferred over '사다' (to buy)
literally 'cat's bathroom'; the everyday word for a litter box
'집사' (butler) is a popular self-deprecating term cat owners use
examples: Cats don't need to be walked.
'산책을 시키다' = to make (a pet) take a walk
If you want a cat, you need litter.
I call myself my cat's servant.
playful '집사' culture is huge among Korean cat owners
nuance: '반려묘' is the formal/written counterpart to '반려견,' but in everyday conversation most people just say '고양이.' The word carries the same respectful 'companion' nuance and shows up in vet clinics, pet shops, and official notices. Cat owners affectionately call themselves '집사' (butler) because cats are seen as the ones in charge.
mistakes: Saying '애완묘' — like '애완견,' it sounds dated; use '반려묘' or just '고양이'
Forgetting that '반려묘' is rarely used in casual chat where '고양이' is normal

usage: the basic verb for feeding kibble
prefix the animal name to specify the food type
'바꾸다' (to change) is used when changing brands or types
examples: I recently switched to a new food.
'새 걸로' = to a new one, '것으로' contracted
We're all out of cat food.
This kibble is good because the pieces are small.
nuance: '사료' is the standard word for processed pet food (both dry kibble and wet food) and also for livestock feed, so context tells you which. For pet treats you switch to a different word entirely ('간식'). When shopping you'll constantly see '건식 사료' (dry) versus '습식 사료' (wet) on packaging.
mistakes: Calling pet treats '사료' — treats are '간식,' while '사료' is the main daily meal
Using '음식' (human food) for pet food; '사료' is the correct term for animals

usage: '하다' is the casual verb for putting a leash on
'착용 필수' = wearing is mandatory; common sign in parks
examples: 밖에 나갈 때는 꼭 목줄을 채워야 해요.
You must put a leash on when going outside.
leashing is legally required in public in Korea
You can't let your dog off-leash in the park.
nuance: '목줄' literally means 'neck rope' and covers both the collar and the walking leash in everyday speech, though the long walking part is sometimes called '리드줄' or just '줄.' In Korea leashing your dog in public is the law, so you'll see '목줄 착용 필수' signs everywhere. A harness (worn on the body, not the neck) is a separate word, '하네스' or '가슴줄.'
mistakes: Confusing '목줄' with '하네스/가슴줄' (body harness) — '목줄' goes around the neck
Using '끈' (general string) instead of '목줄' for a pet leash

usage: '하다' here means to receive/administer the shot
'맞다' (to be struck by) is the verb for getting any shot
vets keep a '기록' (record) you may need for boarding
examples: I took my dog to the vet for shots.
'맞히다' = to have someone receive a shot (causative of 맞다)
The rabies vaccine has to be done every year.
Please show me the vaccination record.
boarding facilities and groomers often ask for this
nuance: '예방접종' (preventive inoculation) is the full, slightly formal term used at clinics; in casual speech people often just say '접종' or '주사' (shot). Note the causative '맞히다' when you take your pet to get a shot, versus '맞다' when the animal itself receives it. Rabies ('광견병') vaccination is legally mandatory and renewed yearly in Korea.
mistakes: Mixing up '맞다' (the pet gets the shot) with '맞히다' (you have the pet get the shot)
Saying '백신을 먹다' — vaccines are '맞다' (received by injection), not eaten

usage: '시키다' makes it causative; written solid — you arrange it for the pet
'여부' = whether; asked on adoption and boarding forms
examples: the surgery is standard for indoor cats
보호소에서 중성화를 한 뒤에 입양 보내요.
The shelter neuters them before adopting them out.
many shelters require this; '입양 보내다' = to rehome
They say neutering makes them calmer.
nuance: '중성화' literally means 'making neutral' and is the gender-neutral umbrella term for both spaying females and neutering males — Korean doesn't usually split the two words in everyday speech. It's almost always said as '중성화 수술' (neutering surgery). Shelters and TNR (trap-neuter-return) programs for street cats use this exact word.
mistakes: Forgetting to add '수술' — '중성화 수술' sounds more complete and natural
Assuming separate male/female terms; '중성화' covers both sexes

usage: '보내다' = to send off, used by the giving side
the '입양 vs 구매' debate is well known in Korea
examples: I adopted a cat from a shelter.
a famous Korean animal-welfare slogan ('사지 말고 입양하세요')
새끼 고양이를 입양 보낼 곳을 찾고 있어요.
I'm looking for a home to adopt out the kittens.
'입양 보낼 곳' = a place to send them for adoption
nuance: '입양' is the same word used for adopting a child, and applying it to pets reflects the modern view that animals are family, not products. The slogan '사지 말고 입양하세요' (adopt, don't shop) is widely recognized. Note the directional pair: you '입양하다' (adopt in) a pet, but you '입양 보내다' (adopt out) when rehoming one.
mistakes: Confusing direction: '입양하다' is receiving a pet, '입양 보내다' is giving one away
Using '사다' (buy) when '입양하다' is the more appropriate, kinder word for shelter pets

usage: '출신' = originating from; describes a dog's background
examples: Our dog used to be a stray.
past tense '-이었어요' for a former state
I volunteer at an abandoned-dog shelter.
If you find a stray dog, report it.
you can report to a shelter or 120 hotline
nuance: '유기견' (abandoned dog) specifically means a dog that was deserted by its owner, distinct from '들개' (a feral/wild dog) born on the streets. The cat equivalent is '유기묘,' and '길고양이' (street cat) is the gentler everyday word for community cats. Adopting a '유기견' carries positive social weight in Korea given strong animal-welfare awareness.
mistakes: Confusing '유기견' (abandoned by an owner) with '들개' (truly feral dog)
Misreading the 유기- prefix — it means 'abandoned,' unrelated to '유기농' (organic)

usage: '갈다' = to grind/file; what cats do on scratchers
a cue that it's time for a trim
one word from 깎다 + -이; '손톱깎이' for human nails
examples: I trim my dog's nails myself.
The cat sharpens its claws on the sofa.
발톱이 너무 길면 다칠 수 있어요.
If the nails get too long, it can get hurt.
overgrown claws can curl and injure the paw
nuance: '발톱' covers both human toenails and animal claws — the same word, with context deciding which. For pets it pairs with '깎다' (trim) for grooming and '갈다' (sharpen/grind) for a cat scratching. A fingernail/finger-claw is '손톱'; '발톱' is specifically the foot/paw.
mistakes: Using '손톱' (fingernail) for an animal's foot claws; paws take '발톱'
Mixing up '깎다' (trim them yourself) with '갈다' (the cat sharpening them)

usage: the verb form for going through shedding
'철' = season; spring and fall are the heavy ones
examples: 요즘 털갈이 철이라 털이 많이 빠져요.
It's shedding season, so there's a lot of hair coming off.
털갈이할 때는 빗질을 자주 해 주세요.
nuance: '털갈이' combines '털' (fur) and '갈이' (changing/replacing) and means the seasonal coat change when pets shed old fur. It peaks in spring and fall, so you'll hear '봄/가을 털갈이 철.' During this time owners brush more and use a '빗' (brush) to control loose fur ('빠진 털').
mistakes: Saying '털이 갈다' — the noun is the fixed compound '털갈이,' used with '하다'
Confusing '털갈이' (shedding fur) with '탈모' (hair loss/balding), which implies a problem

usage: the basic phrase for a vet visit
'데려가다' = to take a living being along
useful when searching on a map app
'24시' = open around the clock, for emergencies
examples: My cat was sick so I took it to the vet.
'데려가다' is for animals/people, '가져가다' is for objects
Is there a vet clinic near here?
handy question for a new resident
If it's an emergency at night, find a 24-hour vet.
nuance: '동물병원' literally means 'animal hospital' and is the standard word for any vet clinic, big or small — there's no separate casual term. Crucially, you '데려가다' (take along, for living things) a pet there, never '가져가다' (carry, for objects). For overnight emergencies look for a '24시 동물병원,' common in larger cities.
mistakes: Using '가져가다' (carry an object) instead of '데려가다' (take a living being) for your pet
Calling it '수의사 병원' — the place is '동물병원'; '수의사' is the vet (the person)

usage: '갈다' = to replace, used for a soiled pad
'훈련' = training; teaching a puppy to use the pad
have an accident off the pad
'실수하다' = to make a mistake, i.e., go in the wrong spot
examples: The dog goes nicely on the pee pad.
'싸다' = to poop/pee, casual but standard for pets
You have to change the pee pad every day.
'갈아 주다' = to change (for the pet's benefit)
nuance: '배변패드' combines '배변' (defecation/elimination) with '패드' (pad) and is the standard product name for the absorbent pads apartment-dwelling dog owners use indoors. It pairs with '깔다' (lay it out) and '갈다' (replace the soiled one). Because most Koreans live in apartments, indoor '배변패드 훈련' is extremely common rather than relying on outdoor walks alone.
mistakes: Using '깔다' (lay out a fresh pad) and '갈다' (replace a used pad) interchangeably — they describe different steps
Saying '기저귀' (diaper, worn on the body) for a floor pad; the floor product is '배변패드'
